vacant.e: From Old French vacant, from Latin vacāns.

vagabond.e: From Old French vagabond, from Late Latin vagābundus, from Latin vagari (“wander”).
vagabond.g: A person on a trip of indeterminate destination and/or length of time.

vail.e: From Middle English vayle, from Old French vail, from valoir (“to be worth”), from Latin valeō (“to be worth”).
From Middle English valen; either from Anglo-Norman valer or a clipping of avalen.

vain.e: From Middle English veyn, from Old French vain, from Latin vānus (“empty”).
vain.g: Overly proud of oneself, especially concerning appearance; having a high opinion of one's own accomplishments with slight reason.

vain.e: A conversion of the adjectival form of vain. The only use of this verb in English appears c. 1628 in the writings of Owen Felltham.

vainglory.e: From Middle English waynglori (“worthless glory”), from Old French vaine glorie, from Medieval Latin vāna glōria, from Latin vāna (“empty, groundless, boastful”) + glōria (“fame, ambition, boasting”), apparently modelled after similar terms in Germanic languages.

vainly.e: From Middle English vaynly, veynly, vaynely, veynely, equivalent to vain + -ly.
vainly.g: In a vain pursuit; to no avail.

vale.e: From Middle English vale, from Old French val (“valley”), from Latin vallis, valles.
Borrowed from Latin valē, singular imperative of valeō (“be well”).

valiant.e: From Middle English vailaunt (“having or showing courage or valour, valiant; characterized by valour; powerful, strong; person of valour or strength; excellent, worthy; beneficial, useful; valuable; legally valid, binding”), from Anglo-Norman vaillaunt, vaylant, and Old French vailant, vaillant (“brave, valiant; having value, valuable”).
valiant.g: Possessing or showing courage or determination; brave, heroic.

valid.e: Borrowed from Middle French valide (“healthy, sound, in good order”), from Latin validus, from valeō (“to be strong, to be healthy, to be worth”) + -idus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“be strong”).

valley.e: From Middle English valeye, valey, from Anglo-Norman valey, Old French valee (compare French vallée), from Latin vallēs/vallis.
valley.g: An elongated depression cast between hills or mountains, often with a river flowing through it.

valour.e: From Middle English valour, from Anglo-Norman valour, from Latin valor.

valuation.e: From Middle French valuation, noun of action from valuer, from Old French valoir.

value.e: From Middle English valew, value, from Old French value, feminine past participle of valoir, from Latin valēre (“be strong, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong”).
value.g: The quality that renders something desirable or valuable; worth.

vanish.e: Aphetic for obsolete evanish, from Middle English evanisshen, esvanisshen, from Old French esvanir, esvaniss- (modern French évanouir), from Vulgar Latin *exvanire (“to vanish, disappear, to fade out”), from Latin ēvānēscō, ēvānēscere, from vānus (“empty”). By surface analysis, Latin vān- + -ish (“verb suffix”).
vanish.g: To become invisible or to move out of view unnoticed.

vanity.e: From va(i)n + -ity, from Middle English vanite, from Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas, from vānus, whence English vain.
vanity.g: That which is vain, futile, or worthless; that which is of no value, use or profit.

vanquish.e: From Middle English venquysshen, vaynquisshen, borrowed from a conjugated form of Old French veincre, from Latin vincō.

vapor.e: From Middle English vapour, from Anglo-Norman vapour, Old French vapor, from Latin vapor (“steam, heat”).
vapor.g: Cloudy diffused matter such as mist, steam or fumes suspended in the air.

variance.e: From Middle English variance, variaunce, equivalent to vary + -ance, from Old French variance or directly from Anglo-Latin variaunce, veriaunce, wariaunce; all from Latin variantia.
variance.g: The act of varying or the state of being variable.

various.e: Borrowed from Middle French varieux, from Latin varius (“manifold, diverse, various, parti-colored, variegated, also changing, changeable, fickle, etc.”). By surface analysis, vary + -ous.
various.g: More than one (of an indeterminate set of things).

vassal.e: From Middle English vassal, from Old French vassal, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from Latin vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).
vassal.g: The grantee of a fief, a subordinate granted use of a superior's land and its income in exchange for vows of fidelity and homage and (typica

vast.e: From Middle French vaste, from Latin vastus (“void, immense”).
vast.g: Very large or wide (literally or figuratively).

vat.e: From Middle English vat, a dialectal variant of fat (“vat, vessel, cask”), from Old English fæt (“vat, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *fat, from Proto-Germanic *fatą (“vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *pod- (“vessel”).
vat.g: A large tub, such as is used for making wine or for tanning.

vault.e: From Middle English vaute, vowte, from Old French volte (modern voûte), from Vulgar Latin *volta < *volvita or *volŭta, a regularization of Latin volūta (compare modern volute (“spire”)), the past participle of volvere (“roll, turn”).
vault.g: An arched masonry structure supporting and forming a ceiling, whether freestanding or forming part of a larger building.

vault.e: Borrowed from Middle French volter (“to turn or spin around; to frolic”), borrowed from Italian voltare, itself from a Vulgar Latin frequentative form of Latin volvere; later assimilated to Etymology 1, above.
vault.g: To jump or leap over with a hand and/or foot on the item for support.

vaunt.e: From Middle English vaunten, from Anglo-Norman vaunter, variant of Old French vanter, from Latin vānus (“vain, boastful”).
